title: Insight Meditation Practice
excerpt: Originally titled Insight Meditation: Basic and Progressive Exercises, by Venerable Mahāsi Sayādaw, translated by Lin Wurui.

inline.s: Originally titled: Insight Meditation: Basic and Progressive Exercises
By Venerable Mahāsi Sayādaw
Translated by Lin Wurui

Everyone knows the principle that people seek pleasure and shun pain. In this world, human beings do all they can to avoid and diminish suffering and to enjoy happiness and joy. Yet the direction of their efforts is mainly to secure the welfare of the physical body by material means, little realizing that happiness depends on the attitude of the mind; only a few truly set their sights on spiritual development, and fewer still strive tirelessly at the training of the mind.

To illustrate this, we may note people’s worldly habits of tending and serving the body; their ceaseless pursuit of clothing, food, and housing; and the astonishing advances in technology made to raise the standard of material life, improve transport and communication, and avoid and cure disease. All these efforts are chiefly concerned with nourishing and maintaining the body. We must grant that they are most basic. Yet human effort and achievement cannot lessen or uproot the suffering that comes with aging, illness, family strife, and the anxieties of livelihood; in short, such pursuits carry within them the insatiability of need and desire. These sufferings cannot be overcome by material means, but only by training the mind and developing wisdom.
The right method, then, plainly must be through the training, calming, and purification of the mind. We find this method in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (see
The Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta

), a very famous discourse spoken by the Buddha more than two thousand five hundred years ago. In that discourse the Buddha taught thus: “This is the sole path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the attainment of the right way, and for the realization of nirvāṇa: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.”

If you sincerely wish to practice meditation and attain insight wisdom in this very life, you must set aside worldly views and ways during the training period. This period of training is for the purification of body and mind, and pure conduct is the first step toward right concentration. You must also observe the precepts of the laity (those who have gone forth should follow the monastic precepts accordingly), for if insight wisdom is to be realized, the precepts are of vital importance.

These precepts, undertaken voluntarily, are: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, not to take intoxicants, not to eat after midday, not to wear garlands or scents, not to watch singing and dancing, and not to sit or lie on high or large beds. One further precept is that in speech you must not belittle, mock, or harbor ill will toward noble ones who have attained the fruits of the path.

The great masters of old would guide practitioners to take refuge in the great Awakened One, the Buddha, during the meditation period, for if impure or terrifying images arise in your mind during practice, you may be frightened by them. You should also follow the guidance of your teacher, for he will truthfully tell you how your practice stands and give you the necessary guidance at the right time.

The greatest benefit and goal of this training is the removal of greed, hatred, and delusion, for they are the root of all evil and suffering. The intensive insight meditation course here can bring you to liberation; therefore, bearing its benefits in mind, you should give it your whole strength, so that your practice may be fully and successfully completed. The meditation method we teach is based on the four foundations of mindfulness, the practice adopted by the great Blessed One and by accomplished disciples of the Buddha through the ages. You should count yourself fortunate, for you have the opportunity to practice by the very same method they used.

Before you begin the practice, you may reflect on the “four protections” taught by the Buddha; they are of immense psychological benefit. These four protections are the recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, the impurity of the body, and death.

First, you must devoutly take refuge in the Buddha and praise his nine qualities: “The Buddha is holy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, worthy of offerings (an arhat), knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of persons, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.”

Second, contemplate your loving-kindness extending to all living beings; all beings receive the blessing of your compassion, and there is no difference between you and them: “May I be free from hatred, disease, and sorrow. As I am, so may my parents, my precept master, and my teachers, and all beings whether near or distant, or harboring ill will, be free from hatred, disease, and sorrow. May all beings be free from the sea of suffering.”

Third, contemplate the filth and impurity of the body, to help you lessen your greedy attachment to it, the thing so many people find hardest to let go. Contemplate the impurity of its various parts, such as the stomach, the intestines, phlegm, pus, and blood; thus the blind craving for the body can be removed.

Fourth, a mental preparation beneficial to you is to recollect that death is a certainty. The Buddha’s teaching stresses that life is uncertain and death is certain; life is fragile, death is unavoidable, and the end of life is death. Life involves birth, aging, illness, and suffering, and finally death; these are the full scope of its existence.

When we begin sitting meditation, we take a seated posture with both legs crossed. You may also leave the legs uncrossed, simply resting them flat on the floor without letting one leg press on the other; this may be more comfortable for you. Please ask your meditation teacher to explain the sitting posture in detail.
If sitting on the floor always seems to hinder your meditation, simply sit in a more comfortable posture. Now please practice according to each of the following steps.

Place your attention (not your eyes) on the abdomen, and you will notice its rising and falling. If at first you cannot perceive it, you may place both hands on the abdomen to feel its movement. Later, the rise on the in-breath and the fall on the out-breath will become evident. Then the mind notes: when the abdomen rises, know “rising”; when the abdomen falls, know “falling”; note each movement as it occurs. This exercise lets you truly feel the abdomen moving up and down, but it does not mean that you should watch the shape of the abdomen; rather, it lets you truly feel the physical pressure produced by its slow movement. So simply practice in this way, and there is no need to attend to the shape of the abdomen.

For a beginner this is a very effective way to cultivate awareness, concentration, and insight in meditation. As your practice deepens, the sensation of the abdominal movement will become more and more distinct.

Only when the power of insight meditation is fully developed are we able to see the whole stream of physical and mental changes at our six sense doors. Because you are a beginner, your powers of alertness and concentration are still weak, and you may feel that it is hard to keep the mind on each rising and falling as it happens. When such difficulties come, you will easily think, “I really do not know how to keep my mind on each rising and falling of the abdomen.” At such times you must remember that this is only a process of learning; the rising and falling of the abdomen is always there, and there is no need to go looking for it.

In fact, for a beginner, keeping the mind on the two movements of the abdomen, “rising” and “falling,” is quite easy to do. Continue this practice, keeping fully alert to the rising and falling of the abdomen.

You must never say “rising” and “falling” aloud, nor visualize the words “rising” and “falling”; just attend to the actual process of the abdomen rising and falling. Nor should you deliberately breathe deeply or rapidly to make the abdominal movement clearer, for doing so brings fatigue and actually disturbs your practice. Simply, with normal breathing, attend wholly to the rising and falling movement.

When you are wholly absorbed in the exercise of observing the abdominal movement, other mental factors will often appear within your noting of each rising and falling. Thoughts and other mental phenomena, such as intentions, ideas, and imaginings, arise easily while you are noting “rising” and “falling.” None of these may be ignored; when they appear, you must note them, naming each one silently.

If you imagine something, the mind must clearly know that it is “imagining.” If you merely recall something, you must note that you are “recalling.” When you reflect, note “reflecting.” When you want to do something, note “wanting.” If the mind strays from the object of concentration and no longer attends to the rising and falling of the abdomen, you should be alert that you are “distracted.” If you imagine going somewhere, note “going”; when you arrive, note “arriving.” If you meet someone in a thought, note “meeting”; if you speak with another, note “speaking, speaking.” If you imagine arguing with someone, note that you are “arguing.” If you visualize or imagine light or color, you must note that you are “seeing, seeing.” Whenever any mental factor appears, you must note it until it passes away. When it has passed, return to Basic Exercise One, knowing fully and being fully alert to each rising and falling movement of the abdomen.

Follow the steps carefully and do not be slack. If you want to swallow saliva and are about to do so, note “wanting.” At the moment of swallowing, note “swallowing, swallowing.” If you want to spit, note “wanting.” At the moment of spitting, note “spitting, spitting.” Then return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you want to bend your neck, note “wanting.” As you bend, note “bending, bending.” If you want to straighten your neck, note “straightening, straightening.” In bending and straightening the neck, the movement must be slow. Every movement you make must be watched with care, and then you return to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen with full clarity.

If you must remain in one posture for a long time, whether sitting or lying down, the body, hands, and feet will feel strong fatigue or stiffness. When this happens, simply place the mind on those parts and note their “fatigue” or “stiffness,” then continue sitting. Note them naturally, neither impatiently nor sluggishly. These feelings will gradually weaken and finally vanish altogether. If some sensations instead grow stronger, and the fatigue of the body and the stiffness of the joints become unbearable, you may change posture. But before you prepare to change posture, do not forget to note “wanting” with care, and every detail of each movement must be observed in its proper sequence.

If you want to raise a hand or lift a foot, note “wanting” in the mind. At the moment of raising the hand or lifting the foot, note “raising, raising.” When bending, note “bending, bending.” When putting it down, note “putting down, putting down.” When the hand or foot touches the body or the ground, note “touching, touching.” All movements should be slow and careful. Once you are settled in the new posture, continue observing the movement of the abdomen. If the new posture makes you hot and uncomfortable and you want to shift to another posture, still proceed slowly according to the steps given in this section.

If any part of the body itches, focus on that part and note “itching, itching.” Do it step by step, neither impatiently nor sluggishly. Throughout the whole process, with exceptionally clear alertness, when the itching sensation passes, continue the practice of observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. If the itch persists and grows stronger, so that you want to scratch that place, you must note “wanting, wanting.” Slowly raise your hand, noting “raising, raising,” and when the hand touches that place, note “touching, touching.” Scratch slowly, fully aware that you are “scratching, scratching.” When the itch is gone and you intend to stop scratching, be clear-minded and, in your usual way, note “wanting, wanting.” As the hand is slowly withdrawn, note “withdrawing, withdrawing.” When the hand rests again where it usually rests by your side, note “touching, touching.” Then continue to focus on the movement of the abdomen.

If there is pain or an unpleasant sensation, place the mind where it arises. As each particular sensation occurs, note whether it is pain, itch, pressure, stinging, tiredness, drowsiness, and so on. It must be stressed here that “noting it” should be neither too forceful nor too slow; the process must go forward in a calm and natural way. The pain will in the end subside or increase. If it increases, do not panic; keep working steadily, and if you can do so, you will find that it always ceases. But if after some time the pain has grown almost unbearable, pay it no heed and continue observing the rising and falling of the abdomen.

As mindfulness strengthens, you may experience certain intense sensations, such as severe pain, difficulty in breathing, or suffocation; pain like being cut by a knife; discomfort as if pierced by something sharp, pricked by a very fine needle, or crawled over by small insects; you may also feel itching, being bitten by something, or intense cold. Once you stop sitting, these sensations stop; but when you resume sitting with clear alertness, they appear again. These painful feelings are nothing to worry about; they are not a sign of illness, but common phenomena of the body that ordinarily go unnoticed because our minds are drawn to more obvious things. The sharper your mental power, the more you can feel them. When your meditation reaches a certain stage, you will be able to overcome them, and they will vanish completely. If you keep sitting with firm resolve, you will meet with no harm. But if you lose your zeal and stop sitting for a while, you will again and again undergo these unpleasant sensations in the course of your practice. If you hold firm without giving up, it is very likely that you will pass beyond these painful sensations and no longer experience them in later sittings.

If you want to sway the body, note “wanting, wanting.” At the moment of swaying, note “swaying, swaying.” In sitting you may occasionally find the body swaying back and forth; do not be alarmed, and neither delight in it nor wish for it to continue. If you turn your mind to the swaying and keep noting “swaying, swaying,” it will stop. If you have noted it and the swaying instead grows worse, then lean against a wall or a pillar, or lie down for a while, and afterwards continue sitting. If you find yourself shaking or trembling, follow the same steps. As your practice advances, you may sometimes feel trembling or chills passing through the back or over the whole body; this is a most blissful phenomenon, which arises naturally when concentration is very good. When you are absorbed in concentration, even a faint sound may startle you. This happens because, when concentration is very good, your sense faculties become all the more acute.

If you feel thirsty while sitting, note that you are “thirsty, thirsty.” When you want to stand up, note “wanting, wanting.” As you prepare to stand, note every movement. At the moment of rising, be very attentive and note “rising, rising.” When you prepare to walk forward, note “wanting, wanting.” As you begin to step forward, note every step, such as “walking, walking,” or “left, right.” It is important to note every movement of every step from the first to the last. In walking meditation or in the practice of walking, keep closely to each stage of the procedure. Try dividing each step into two movements, noting “lifting the foot, putting it down; lifting the foot, putting it down.” If you have become skilled in this way of training in walking, try dividing it into three stages, noting “lifting, moving, putting down,” or “raising, advancing, putting down.”
When you walk to the place where tea is kept and see the water dispenser or the teapot, remember to note that you are “seeing, seeing.”
When you stop, note “stopping, stopping.”
When you reach out your hand, note “reaching, reaching.”
When your hand touches the cup, note “touching, touching.”
When you pick up the cup, note “picking up, picking up.”
When you pour water with the cup, note “pouring water, pouring water.”
When you bring the cup to your lips, note “bringing, bringing.”
When the cup touches your lips, note “touching, touching.”
When the water touches you and feels cold, note “cold, cold.”
When you swallow the water, note “swallowing, swallowing.”
When you put the cup back, note “putting back, putting back.”
When you withdraw your hand, note “withdrawing the hand, withdrawing the hand.”
When you lower your hand, note “lowering, lowering.”
When your hand touches the side of your body, note “touching, touching.”
When you want to turn back, note “wanting, wanting.”
As you turn, note “turning, turning.”
As you walk forward, note “walking, walking.”
When you reach the place where you want to stop, note “wanting, wanting.”
After stopping, note “stopping, stopping.”

If you remain standing for a moment, continue observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you intend to sit down, note “wanting, wanting.” As you walk forward preparing to sit, note “walking, walking.” When you reach the seat, note “arriving, arriving.” As you turn to sit down, note “turning, turning.” At the moment of the sitting movement, note “sitting, sitting.” Sit down slowly, keeping aware of the slow movements of the body. As you arrange your hands and feet, note every detail of the movement. Then return to your original practice and observe the rising and falling of the abdomen.

If you want to lie down, note “wanting, wanting.” Then, following the stages of meditation, note the whole process of lying down: “rising from the seat, stretching out, moving away, touching the bed, lying down.” When your hands, feet, and body are in place, take every movement as an object to be noted in meditation. Make each movement slowly, then continue observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. If pain, fatigue, itch, or other sensations arise, you must note them one by one. Note all feelings, thoughts, conceptions, thinking, and reflection, and all movements of the hands, feet, arms, and body. If there is nothing in particular to observe, rest the mind on the rising and falling of the abdomen. When drowsy, note “drowsy”; when sleepy, note “sleepy.” When your power of concentration is sufficient, you will overcome drowsiness and sleepiness and feel fresh and clear. Rouse your energy again and practice according to the basic steps. If you truly cannot overcome sleepiness, keep observing until you fall asleep.

The state of sleep is a continuation of the subconscious. It is very similar to the consciousness that first arises at rebirth and to the consciousness of the final moment at death. The consciousness at such times is very weak, and so it cannot be observed. When you are awake, in the intervals between seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, touching, and thinking, the subconscious still occurs regularly; it is simply too brief, and ordinarily it is neither clear nor easy to notice. It continues throughout sleep, and when you wake it becomes inconspicuous, because while awake thoughts and the objects we are to observe are more prominent.

Meditation should begin from the moment you wake, though as a beginner you may not be able to manage this. But as soon as the thought occurs to you, you must apply yourself at once. For example, as soon as you notice that you are turning something over in your mind, you must be alert to that fact and begin noting inwardly, “thinking, thinking.” Then return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. When you get up, you must be alert to every subtle movement of the body; every detail of the hands and feet must be moved in a state of full wakefulness. On waking, are you thinking about what time it is? If so, note “thinking, thinking.” Are you planning to get out of bed? If so, note “wanting, wanting.” If you are preparing to shift your body into the posture for rising, note “preparing, preparing.” As you slowly get up, note “rising, rising.” When you are in a sitting posture, note “sitting, sitting.” If you remain sitting for some time, switch to noting the rising and falling of the abdomen.

When washing your face or taking a bath, perform every small movement in full alertness; for example, note “looking, looking; seeing, seeing; reaching, reaching; taking, taking; touching, touching; feeling cold, feeling cold; wiping, wiping.” When dressing, making the bed, opening or closing doors and windows, or picking things up, be attentive to every detail of each movement.
While eating, every subtle movement must be observed.
When you look at the food, note “looking, looking.”
When you set out the dishes, note “setting out, setting out.”
When you bring food to your mouth, note “bringing, bringing.”
When you bend your neck forward, note “bending, bending.”
When the food touches your lips, note “touching, touching.”
When you put the food into your mouth, note “putting in, putting in.”
When you close your mouth, note “closing, closing.”
When you withdraw your hand, note “withdrawing, withdrawing.”
If your hand touches the plate, note “touching, touching.”
When you straighten your neck, note “straightening, straightening.”
When you chew, note “chewing, chewing.”
When you know a taste, note “knowing, knowing.”
When you swallow the food, note “swallowing, swallowing.”
When the food is swallowed and touches the throat, note “touching, touching.”

Observe in this way with every small mouthful you eat, until the meal is finished. At the beginning you may leave out many details; do not mind this, and do not be discouraged. If you keep practicing steadily, the omissions will gradually decrease. When your level is higher, you will notice movements more subtle than those we have described here.

After every forty to ninety minutes of sitting, you may practice walking meditation, alternating the two. This helps to balance calm and energetic effort so as to overcome drowsiness. You may practice on a quiet path or in a room; the best way is to walk more slowly than usual. Walking slowly is ideal, though it should be done in a simple and natural manner. In walking meditation, focus on the movements of the feet and legs. When the right foot begins to step, note “lifting the foot”; as it moves, note “moving”; as it is put down, note “putting down.” Do the same with the left foot.

Just as in the method of observing the in-breath and out-breath while sitting, all distracting thoughts or feelings should be noted and dealt with. In walking meditation, if the eyes glance aside, you should at once become aware of “glancing” and return to noting the movement of the feet. See every detail clearly, even movements that do not belong to the walking exercise as such. If, for instance, a glance occurs unintentionally, note “glancing.”

When you reach the end of the path you must turn around and walk in the opposite direction; you will notice this two or three steps before you get there. You must note the intention to turn. At first it may be hard to notice, but when your concentration is strong enough you will see it. After seeing the intention to turn, you should also note the other related thoughts and movements at the moment of turning. When you have taken the last step and are truly about to turn, note “turning”; when one foot lifts, note “lifting the foot, turning, putting down,” and the same with the other foot. Then, as you set off walking back, note “lifting the foot, moving, putting down.” Often there is an irresistible temptation to look for something interesting to see; when such untrained impulses arise, you should note “wanting to look,” and you will naturally return to the movement of the feet.

For a beginner, the best way to practice walking meditation is usually to observe in three stages as described above: “lifting the foot, moving, putting down.” Your teacher will also teach you to divide it into more or fewer stages according to your ability. Sometimes walking too slowly is inconvenient, especially when practicing meditation outdoors; in that case, simply note “left, right; left, right.” The point is not how many stages you observe, but whether you truly take note of the physical and mental phenomena at the moment they occur, or whether your mind is merely blank.

After repeated practice you may find that your proficiency has improved considerably, and that your concentration lasts longer when you do the basic observation of the rising and falling of the abdomen. At this point you will notice that there is usually a slight pause between “rising” and “falling.” If you are sitting, note the sitting posture during that pause, as in “rising, falling, sitting.” While noting “sitting,” place the mind on the upright upper body. If you are lying down, follow the same steps, noting with full alertness “rising, falling, lying.” If you find this easy to do, continue noting these three stages. If you find that there is a pause both after “rising” and after “falling,” continue in the manner “rising, sitting, falling, sitting.” Or, when lying down, “rising, lying, falling, lying.” When you find that the three or four stages described above are no longer easy to do, return to the original way of practice and note only “rising, falling.”

In doing the regular exercise of observing the body, there is no need to attend to images and sounds; as long as you can keep the mind on noting the rising and falling of the abdomen, you will naturally observe them. Still, you may want to look at some object; in that case you may note “seeing, seeing” two or three times, and then return to noticing the movement of the abdomen. If an image of someone appears, also note “seeing, seeing,” and then return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. Have you ever overheard a sound by accident? Did you listen to it at the time? If so, note “listening, listening,” and after that movement, return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. If you hear a loud sound, such as a dog barking or people talking or singing, at once note “hearing, hearing” two or three times, and then return to the basic exercise of observing the rising and falling of the abdomen.

When conspicuous images and sounds appear, if you cannot be alert to them and let them pass, you will follow them into associations and be unable to observe the rising and falling of the abdomen continuously. The rising and falling of the abdomen may then become less clear. And it is precisely when our attention is weak that the emotions which defile the mind are able to grow and multiply. If associations arise, note inwardly two or three times, “associating, associating,” and then rouse yourself to observe the rising and falling of the abdomen. If the hands, feet, or body move and you forget to notice it, note inwardly “forgetting, forgetting,” and then return to the usual observation of the abdominal movement.

Sometimes the breathing may feel slow, or you may be unable to feel the rising and falling of the abdomen clearly. When this happens, if you are sitting, simply continue noting “sitting, sitting; touching, touching”; if you are lying down, note “lying, lying; touching, touching.” In observing “touching,” do not rest the mind on one fixed part of the body, but note the various different parts of the body in order. The body has several points of contact, and there are at least six or seven places that should be observed: the contact of the thighs with the knees, the two hands resting one upon the other, or finger against finger, thumb against thumb, the opening and closing of the eyelids, the tongue within the mouth, or the upper and lower lips touching.

By now you have been attending this training course for a considerable time. It is quite possible that, finding you have not made much progress, you begin to feel slack. In any case, do not give up halfway; simply note “slackness, slackness.” Until attention, concentration, and insight have been sufficiently cultivated, you may doubt the correctness and efficacy of this method of training. If such a state arises, you should go back to observing the thought of “doubt, doubt.” Do you expect or hope for good results? If so, take these thoughts as objects of meditation observation: “expecting, expecting,” or “hoping, hoping.” Are you trying to recall the methods of training you have used up to now? If so, observe “recollecting, recollecting.” And at that time, are you examining the object you are observing to judge whether it belongs to the mental or the physical? Then note “examining, examining.” Are you disappointed that you have made no progress? If so, note the feeling of disappointment. Conversely, are you glad of your progress? If so, observe the feeling of happiness.
This method is simply this: when each state of mind occurs, note it; if no thought intervenes and no sensation arises, return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen.

During a strict meditation course, the time of practice runs from the moment you wake in the morning until you fall asleep at night. To stress it again: throughout the whole day, including the night, except for the few hours of sleep, you must continually do the basic exercise of observing the abdomen, noting and observing with clarity, without any slackness. When meditation reaches a certain stage, even if you lengthen your hours of practice, you will not feel like sleeping; on the contrary, you will be able to keep it up day and night.

In this short course of training we have stressed that whenever a wholesome or unwholesome state arises, or whenever any limb moves, whether the movement is large or subtle, or whenever any pleasant or painful physical or mental feeling arises, it should be observed. If during practice there is nothing in particular worth noting, return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen with full attention. When you must walk to do anything, every step should be fully clear, and you should simply note “walking, walking,” or “left, right.” In practicing walking meditation, every step must be noted as “lifting, moving, putting down.” If a trainee in this course practices diligently day and night, before long he can reach the first stage of the four insights (experiencing arising and passing away), and then advance toward a higher level of insight meditation.

As described above, through diligent practice alertness and concentration have grown stronger. The meditator then finds that “the object observed” and “the awareness of it” arise in pairs, such as “rising” and “knowing that it rises,” “falling” and “knowing that it falls,” “sitting” and “knowing that one sits,” “bending the arm” and “knowing the bending movement,” “extending the arm” and “knowing the extending movement,” “lifting the foot” and “knowing the lifting movement,” “putting the foot down” and “knowing the putting-down movement.” Through one-pointed attention he knows how to distinguish each process of body and mind: “Rising is one process, and knowing that it rises is another process; falling is one process, and knowing that it falls is another process.” He understands that “the awareness of it” has the characteristic of “tending toward an object.” This can be explained as the quality of our mind’s function of “inclining toward an object” or “cognizing an object.” We must know that the more clearly a physical object presents itself, the more clearly the mind observes it. On this point the Visuddhimagga says:
When materiality is evident, clear, and translucent, the mentality that takes materiality as its object becomes correspondingly clear and refined.”

When the meditator knows the difference between the activity of the body and the activity of the mind, if he is a simple person he will directly experience from this: “Rising and knowing it; falling and knowing it,” and nothing else besides; there is no designation of “man” or “woman,” nor any word for “person” or “soul.” If he is a widely learned person, he will directly realize, between the materiality of the object and the mental activity that knows it: “Here there is only body and mind; apart from these there is no so-called individual man or woman. In observation one can find that there is a physical phenomenon as object, and a mental activity that knows it; this pair of mental and physical activities is what is conventionally called a ‘being,’ a ‘person,’ or a ‘soul,’ a ‘man’ or a ‘woman.’” But apart from this twofold process of body and mind, there is no other person or being, self or other, man or woman. When the meditator finds that he is reflecting on these principles, he must note “reflecting, reflecting,” and then return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen.

As meditation progresses, it becomes clearly evident that before a bodily movement occurs, there is first a volitional activity in the consciousness. The meditator first notices that volitional activity. Although at the beginning of practice he did notice “wanting, wanting” (for example, when bending the arm), he still could not clearly notice the state of consciousness. Now, because his proficiency has advanced another step, he clearly notices the “volition” in the consciousness that wants to bend the arm; so he first notices the volition, and then observes the bodily movement that follows.

At the beginning, because he neglected to note the volitional activity, he thought that the bodily movement was faster than the mind that knows it. At this stage he discovers that the mind is the forerunner. The meditator notices at all times the volition that precedes bending, stretching, sitting, standing, coming and going, and so on. He also clearly notices the actual process of bending, stretching, and the rest. Thus he understands that the formations of the mind precede the movements of the body. He directly experiences that bodily movement occurs following upon volitional activity.

Moreover, he realizes directly from experience that when he notes “heat, heat” or “cold, cold,” they grow stronger. In observing the regular and natural bodily movements such as the rising and falling of the abdomen, he notes them one after another, continuously. He also notices images of the Buddha or of arhats that surface in the mind, and when any sensation (such as pain, itch, or heat) arises, he notices directly where it arises. Before one sensation has passed, another arises, and he notices each of them. Noting these phenomena as they arise, he perceives that the mind’s process of cognizing arises in dependence on the arising of the phenomena. Sometimes the rising and falling of the abdomen is so subtle that there is no object to note; then he realizes that if there is no object to note, the act of cognizing cannot arise.

If there is no rising and falling to note (translator’s note: because body and mind have become still), then you should note “sitting” and “touching,” or “lying” and “touching,” and alternate between them. For example, after noting “sitting, sitting,” note the sensation of touch that arises where the right foot contacts the ground or the cushion. Then, after noting “sitting, sitting,” note the sensation of touch of the left foot. In the same way, note the sensations of several places. While noting “seeing,” “hearing,” and so on, the meditator clearly knows that “seeing” comes from the contact of the eye with visible form, and “hearing” arises from the contact of the ear with sound, and so forth.

He reflects further: “The stretching and bending of the body occur following upon the mind’s wanting to stretch or bend; the same is true of other movements.” He continues to reflect: “The heat and cold of the body arise because of the elements of heat or cold; the body lives dependent on food and nourishment; consciousness arises in dependence on objects; seeing arises in dependence on visible form; hearing arises in dependence on sound … and there must also be the sense faculties such as the eye and ear; all these are causal conditions. Only when the earlier sense faculties, objects, and consciousness come together do the volition and attention that follow arise; through past karma, from the moment of birth the activities of body and mind begin, and the various feelings of the present come to be. There is no subject that creates this body and mind; everything happens simply because the conditions are complete.” The meditator reflects on these principles while noting any physical or mental phenomenon. He need not stop and take time to think; at the moment of noting each phenomenon as it arises, these reflections come swiftly, as if spontaneously. At such times the meditator must note: “reflecting, reflecting; discerning, discerning,” and then continue observing.

The present physical and mental phenomena arise from the formations of past body and mind, and their nature of dependent origination is the same. Having reflected on this, the meditator reflects further that the states of past body and mind were in turn produced by even earlier conditions, and that future physical and mental phenomena will arise according to the same law. Apart from this process of mutual dependence, there is no separate “individual” or “person” existing independently; there is only “cause” and “effect” proceeding. If such reflections arise, they too must be observed, and one should proceed according to the steps we have learned. Some people with a strong inclination toward rational thinking have countless such occurrences, while those without that inclination have fewer. In any case, whenever reflection arises it should be closely noted. Noting can reduce them to a minimum, so that the progress of insight is not hindered by excessive reflection. One should know that a minimum of reflection is more than enough here.

When the meditator practices meditation diligently, he may experience certain almost unbearable sensations, such as pain, itch, heat, stuffiness, and stiffness. If he pays them no heed, they vanish, but as soon as he resumes observing, they appear again. These sensations are produced by the innate sensitivity of the body; they are not signs of illness, and if he observes them again with diligent attention, they will gradually weaken.

The meditator will sometimes see images as if with his own eyes: for instance, a radiant Buddha, rows of monks in the sky, pagodas and Buddha images, people he loves, forests and plants, high mountains and hills, gardens, towers; he may see himself facing a swollen corpse or a skeleton, dilapidated and collapsed houses, and a dead body scattered in pieces, a bloated corpse covered with blood, dismembered and dispersed, finally a heap of white bones; he may see the large and small intestines, vital organs, even maggots; he may see beings in hell, or people in the heavens, and so on. These are merely images created because intense concentration has sharpened our imagination; they are like images seen in a dream, and there is no need to cling to them with greed, nor to be frightened by them. The things seen during meditation are not real; they are only images or things imagined, yet the mind takes them as real.

However, pure mental activity, if it is not joined with the images of the five sense faculties, is not easy to observe clearly and subtly. Therefore, place the emphasis on those senses that are easy to observe, and then observe the mental activities that arise in connection with them. Hence, whatever image appears must be noted, silently repeating “seeing, seeing” in the mind until it disappears. It will depart, gradually blur, or break apart and scatter. At first it may take five to ten silent repetitions, but when the power of insight grows stronger, only a few are needed and it disappears. However, if the meditator takes delight in the sight, or wants to see it more clearly, or feels fear because of it, it will instead linger. If one deliberately conjures up a certain situation, that situation, because of the meditator’s liking for it, will remain even longer. So when concentration is strong, be careful not to think about or incline toward anything off the subject. As soon as a thought arises, it must be at once noticed and removed. Some people, when meditating, become lazy and slack if there is no special state or sensation; then they must note “laziness, laziness” until it is overcome.

At this stage, whether or not the meditator encounters special states or sensations, he clearly knows the beginning, middle, and final phase of each observation. At the start of practice, when a new situation appeared, he would shift to it and could not clearly notice how the object formerly observed had disappeared. Now he can perceive not only the disappearance of the previous object but also the arising of the next. Thus he has a clear understanding of the beginning, middle, and end of each observed situation.

At this stage the meditator’s proficiency advances another level: he observes that every object arises and vanishes swiftly, and this feeling is so profound that he reflects: “What is born must perish; all things must in the end pass away; no phenomenon can remain forever unchanged; all this is truly impermanent.” This accords with what the Pali scriptures say: “All is impermanent, decaying, unstable.”

He reflects further: “Because of ignorance we cling and delight, yet in truth nothing is delightful, for all things ceaselessly arise and pass away, and we sorrow and lament over them; this is truly a great terror. We may die at any moment; all things must in the end come to an end; this everywhere-present phenomenon of impermanence is indeed fearful and dreadful.” This matches what the scriptures describe: “Whatever is impermanent is suffering and fearful; it is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away.”

Because he has profoundly experienced suffering, he reflects further: “All is suffering, all is decaying.” This accords with the scriptures: “See suffering as a thorn, as a boil, as an arrow.” He reflects further: “This whole mass of suffering cannot be escaped; it arises and passes away, and is unworthy of care or attachment. No one can prevent it from happening; it is not within human power to control, but simply runs on according to natural law.” This confirms what the scriptures say: “Whatever is suffering is without self; what is without self cannot remain unchanged, because one cannot make it thus or prevent it from being thus.” The meditator should note that these reflections have arisen, and observe them accordingly.

Having personally realized these three laws directly from the situations he observes, the meditator by analogy also comprehends that others he has not observed are likewise impermanent, suffering, and without self.

For those things he has not personally realized, he reaches this conclusion: “They too exist according to the same law: impermanent, suffering, without self.” This is inferred from his present experience. Some people are not so strong in understanding, or are more lacking in knowledge, and simply observe without reflecting; in them the above inferences are less evident. But in one who is caught up in reflection, this often happens, sometimes at every observation. Such excessive reflection hinders the progress of insight. At this stage, even if no reflection occurs, the meditator’s realization advances another level, becoming clearer and more profound. Therefore, do not spend effort on reflection. While observing more simply, also take care that when such reflections arise, you do not sink into them.

After realizing the three marks, the meditator no longer reflects much, but simply keeps observing the physical and mental phenomena that continuously present themselves. Then the five mental powers, namely, confidence, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, come into balance, and at this point the faculty of observation speeds up as if roused, and the physical and mental phenomena observed also arise more swiftly. In a brief moment of in-breath, the swelling of the abdomen is a series of rapidly successive movements; the same is true of the subsiding process on the out-breath. This swiftly connected change of movement is also very evident in the stretching and bending of the limbs. There is also a faint vibration throughout the body. In some cases stinging and itching sensations arise in a flash, one after another. Broadly speaking, these sensations are hard to endure.

If the meditator tries to name these feelings, he will not be able to keep up with the speed of this stream of physical and mental changes. It is enough simply to observe with an ordinary attitude, yet he must be clearly alert. At this stage, do not expect to see every subtle point of the swiftly arising situations; just do it in the usual way. If you want to name them, a general term is enough. If you try to keep up closely without missing anything, you will soon be exhausted. What matters is that the observation is clear and that you understand the arisen state. Whereas you formerly chose a few objects to observe, on entering this stage you must set them aside for the time being and attend instead to the situations arising at the six sense doors. Only when your power of observation is not sharp enough to do this should you fall back on the method of the previous stage.

Many times the rapid changes of body and mind are far faster than the blink of an eye or a flash of lightning. But as long as the meditator simply keeps observing these phenomena, he can see the whole process of their occurrence clearly. Because his alertness has become so keen, it seems that no sooner does any phenomenon arise than it is at once noticed, and under the light of awareness they seem to shine, and he can see each one clearly. At this the meditator is deeply convinced: “Body and mind change in an instant, swift as a machine or an engine. Now I have seen it and understood it. Beyond this there is no perplexity; what was to be understood is now understood.” He believes this because he has personally experienced what he had never even dreamed of before.

Furthermore, through the power of insight the meditator may experience radiance, or even rapturous joy, with gooseflesh, streaming tears, trembling limbs, and a subtle vibration and excitement within the body, as if sitting on a swing swaying to and fro, so that he even wonders whether he is merely dizzy. Then the mind becomes peaceful yet lively and alert; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he feels very serene, the activities of body and mind are quite light and nimble, he can observe objects with ease, and he can remain with them as long as he wishes. He no longer feels the body to be stiff, hot, or painful; he sees through every situation serenely, the mind becomes upright and refined, and he wishes to be far from all evil. Because his confidence is unshakable, his mind is bright. Sometimes, when there is no situation needing observation, the mind simply remains in a state of serenity. Reflections such as these arise: “The Buddha truly is the greatly awakened and greatly knowing one; the changes of body and mind are indeed impermanent, suffering, and without self.” As he observes, the three marks are clear to his mind, and he wants to encourage others to practice meditation as well. He is far from laziness and drowsiness, neither slack nor tense, and a serene quietness of mind arises with the power of insight, a joy such as he has never known before. Therefore he wants to share his experience with others. At this time a subtle attachment arises toward this insight and the accompanying radiance, clear mindfulness, and blissful serenity. He experiences these pleasures of concentration.

The meditator should not linger and ponder over these states. Whenever a state presents itself, he should observe: this is “equanimity, confidence, joy, serenity, happiness …” When radiance arises, he should note it until it disappears; other cases should be handled in the same way. When brilliant light first arises, it easily makes one forget to observe and gaze at it with delight; even if one keeps clear awareness while gazing at it, there is still a mixture of rapture and happiness, and one is reluctant to let it go. Later, however, one becomes accustomed to such phenomena and can continue observing them until they disappear. Sometimes the light that appears is so strong that even when one simply and clearly looks at it, it still does not vanish. Then one should stop and shift attention to other phenomena, observing them diligently. One must not go on thinking about whether the light has disappeared; if such a thought arises, one should note it strongly and remove it.

When concentration is very strong, one sees not only light; other extraordinary states also appear, and if one inclines toward any situation, they will persist. If such a tendency arises, the meditator should notice it at once. Sometimes, even without inclining toward a particular state, faint situations appear one after another like a whole train of cars, and toward these visible images the meditator should simply note “seeing, seeing,” and they will vanish one by one. When the power of insight is weaker, the states may become more conspicuous; then one should observe them one by one until these train-like situations finally disappear.

We must understand that toward certain states, for instance being drawn to and captivated by radiance, clinging is the wrong attitude. Facing any state, the right response is to follow the essentials of insight meditation, observing with clarity and without grasping, until they disappear. The meditator continues his awareness of body and mind, and insight grows sharper, seeing more clearly the arising and passing away of physical and mental phenomena, and understanding that each phenomenon arises in its own place and ceases in its own place; the phenomenon that arose before is one thing, and what arises afterwards is another. Thus from each act of awareness he realizes impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Then, after reflecting for a time, he believes: “This truly is the highest state; there is nothing more excellent.” And he becomes complacent about such attainment, easily slackening and stopping. But he must not slacken merely because he has reached such a state; he should continue observing the changes of body and mind for a long period.

As practice advances, wisdom ripens further, and the meditator no longer clearly sees the arising of physical and mental phenomena; he attends only to their disappearance, and the inner process of awareness, because of its swift disappearance, is likewise thus. For example, when he notices the abdomen swelling, the very “movement” of swelling is “born” and at once “ceases”; the same is true of the mind that arises to notice it and then disappears. He understands that the “arising” of a phenomenon and the “noting of it” swiftly follow one another and vanish. The same is seen in observing the subsiding of the abdomen, in sitting, in stretching or bending the arms and legs, and in the stiffness of the limbs. Seeing the arising of a phenomenon and “seeing its cessation” swiftly following one another, some meditators can even clearly distinguish these three processes: noticing the phenomenon, the disappearance of the phenomenon, and the consciousness that recognizes its disappearance also disappearing, all occurring continuously in a single instant. But it is enough if one can know the dissolution of the phenomenon and the corresponding dissolution of the consciousness that notes it.

When the meditator can observe the phenomena described above without interruption, the particular concepts of body, head, hands, and legs become blurred, and all is simply vanishing and dissolving. At this point he may easily feel that his meditation has not yet reached the standard; this is not so. Our minds are used to delighting in clinging to particular forms, and once these forms disappear, the mind lacks satisfaction. In fact this is a manifestation of the progress of insight: at first one clearly observes the characteristics and names of phenomena, and now, because of that progress, one observes their disappearance first. Unless one reflects repeatedly, the “arising” of phenomena will appear again; otherwise their “cessation” will be stronger. The meditator directly experiences the truth stated by the wise: “When name and thinking arise, reality is not seen; when reality appears, name and thinking disappear.”

When the meditator observes clearly, he may think that he is not observing carefully enough. This is because insight is so swift and sharp that even the subconscious momentarily intervening between two acts of recognition cannot hide. He has an impulse to do something, such as bending or stretching an arm, and he at once notices that impulse already tending toward disappearance; as a result, for a time he is unable to make the bending or stretching movement. Then he should turn his attention to one of the six sense doors and continue to observe simply.

Observation should extend over the whole body. Usually one begins with observing the rising and falling of the abdomen, and one can quickly set the energy of observation going continuously again; then one should note “touching” and “knowing the touch,” or “seeing” and “knowing the seeing,” or “hearing” and “knowing the hearing.” Whatever appears, observe that. If this makes you restless or tired, return to observing the rising and falling of the abdomen. After a while, when the continuity of observation is restored, again note whatever phenomenon appears anywhere in the body.

When he can observe all situations well, even without special attention he will understand that what is heard at this moment is passing away, and what is seen is breaking up piece by piece, with no permanence in it. This is seeing things as they really are. Because their vanishing is so swift, some meditators cannot see clearly and feel that their eyesight has weakened or their eyes are blurred. In fact this is not so. Their power of discernment is not sufficient to observe what happens in the preceding and following moments, and so they cannot see the characteristics. Then they should relax and pause their observation. Yet the phenomena of body and mind continue to change, and consciousness continues to attend to them according to its own law. He may not feel like sleeping, or he may be alert and clear yet unable to sleep. Then he need not worry about insomnia, for because of concentration it will not make him uncomfortable or cause him to fall ill. He need only observe diligently and understand that his mind can discern the object to be observed with complete clarity.

He continues to observe the vanishing of both “the phenomenon” and “the cognition of the phenomenon,” and reflects: “Not even for a blink or a flash of lightning is there anything that persists unchanged; formerly I did not understand this. In the past it decayed and dissolved, and in the future it will be so as well.” At this he should note “reflecting,” and moreover, during observation he easily gives rise to fear. He reflects: “Formerly I knew only pleasure and did not know the truth; now, seeing the truth of ceaseless decay and dissolution, I am truly overawed, for with every moment’s change a person may die. This life is dreadful from its very beginning, and so is endless ‘birth.’ Therefore it is futile to try to grasp impermanent, changing phenomena in pursuit of happiness and joy. ‘Birth’ is truly dreadful, and living on in phenomena that ceaselessly decay and dissolve, with aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and grief, is dreadful.” He must note these reflections and let them go.

When the meditator sees that nothing can be relied upon, body and mind become feeble and joyless, and he no longer glows with vigor and high spirits. But he must not be discouraged, for this is a sign of the progress of insight. Nothing is more disheartening than becoming aware of what is dreadful, and he should note such reflections and continue observing the phenomena arising one after another; the unhappy feeling will naturally disappear. If he does not do so, sorrow will take possession of his mind and he will be overcome by fear. Such fear has nothing to do with insight; therefore he should observe diligently and not let it well up in his mind.

In the course of observation he will very likely discover these faults again: “Body and mind are changing, impermanent, and suffering; ‘birth’ is not a good thing, and birth after birth cannot be stilled, and neither is this. Phenomena that once seemed solid and real, once their true face is seen through, are utterly disappointing. In these impermanent, illusory phenomena, to seek happiness and joy is like seeking fish by climbing a tree. Birth is not delightful; aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and grief are dreadful.” When reflections like these arise, they too should be noted.

He readily perceives that the phenomena of body and mind, and the consciousness that is aware of them, are equally coarse, low, and unworthy of delight; seeing their arising and passing away, he feels revulsion, and even sees the body as fragile, decaying, and dissolving.

At this stage the meditator observes all physical and mental phenomena and feels revulsion. Although through a series of keen observations he clearly sees through the illusory and perishable nature of phenomena, he no longer shines with awareness; this is the result of his revulsion, and he appears listless. Yet he cannot simply stop observing; this is like a person walking along a muddy, filthy path, where every step disgusts him, yet he cannot simply stop walking. At this time he regards the human world as a place of inevitable decay, and he no longer rejoices in being reborn as a human being, whether as a man or a woman, a king or a billionaire. He has feelings like those of the heavenly realms.

With this realization, he feels revulsion toward all the physical and mental phenomena he observes, or wishes to be liberated from them. Whatever the movement, whether seeing, hearing, touching, reflecting, standing, sitting, bending, stretching, or noting, he simply wants to abandon all these formations. At this time he should note the arising of “wishing.” He reflects: “With every observation, all these formations are endlessly repeated; this is truly a wretched business. I should stop observing them.” Then he must note such reflections.

Some meditators, after reflecting in this way, stop observing, yet the phenomena of body and mind, such as “rising,” “falling,” “stretching,” “bending,” and “intention,” still proceed as before. So he feels joy: “Though I have stopped observing body and mind, their changing formations still proceed as before, and consciousness automatically notices them too. Therefore liberation cannot be reached merely by stopping observation; the changes of body and mind do not cease because one no longer observes them. One need only, as before, keep watching their arising and passing away, and one can thoroughly realize the three marks, then let go, enter stillness, have all formations stilled, experience nirvāṇa, peace, and joy.” Because of this joy he continues observing. Some meditators who cannot reflect in this way, once they are satisfied after their teacher’s explanation, will likewise continue observing.

After continued observation has entered a favorable phase, some people’s experience at that time gives rise to sensations of pain. They need not be discouraged, for this is merely a characteristic of the whole mass of suffering, as the scriptures say: “Observe the five aggregates as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a thorn, as an affliction, as a torment, and so on.” Even without painful sensations, in each observation one of the three marks, impermanence, suffering, or non-self, will be clearly seen. Although the meditator observes in accordance with the teaching, he still feels it is not perfect, thinking that the consciousness which observes and the object observed are not closely following one another; this is because he is too eager, and so he cannot fully realize the three marks. Dissatisfied with his observation, he keeps changing posture: while sitting, he thinks he could walk better; while walking, he wants to return to sitting; once seated, he wants to adjust his hands and feet, then to move elsewhere, then to lie down; and after each change of posture he cannot remain long, becoming fretful and restless. But he need not be disappointed. It is because he has not yet understood the truth of the dependent origination of body and mind, nor realized the stillness of that dependent origination. He is doing well, yet his feelings run contrary; he should hold to one posture, and afterwards he will find that he can remain settled in it. By continuing to watch the changes of physical and mental phenomena with diligence, the mind will gradually become concentrated and clearly aware, and the fretful feeling will in the end disappear completely.

Once he can face the changes of body and mind calmly, the mind becomes clear and can keenly observe their arising and passing away, as if observing smoothly without any deliberate effort, and even subtle physical and mental phenomena require no exertion. The truths of impermanence, suffering, and non-self appear plainly without any need for reflection. Wherever a sensation arises in the body, the attention falls there, yet that contact feels as soft as wool. Sometimes there are so many points of observation appearing throughout the body that observation must be quickened, and body and mind seem about to be drawn upward; then the sensations feel sparse and scattered, and the meditator can observe them calmly and easily. Sometimes the physical reactions disappear entirely, leaving only the changes of mind, and joy arises like a fine drizzle, intoxicating and filling one with serenity, or one sees a radiance like a clear sky. Yet these special experiences will not shake him or make him dizzy with delight, though he may still enjoy them. At this time he should be alert that he is enjoying such experience; he should note the presence of joy, serenity, and radiance. If these phenomena do not disappear, he need not attend to them, and should turn instead to other phenomena that arise.

Entering this stage, he is wholly convinced of the truth of non-self, knowing that everything is merely the conditioned fabrication of mind and body — one mind-body arising to cognize the phenomena of another. He observes each arising phenomenon with joy and never grows weary with time. He can maintain a single posture for a long while without pain; whether sitting or lying, he is able to sustain observation for two or three hours without the slightest discomfort, and when the session ends his posture remains as steady as at the start.

Sometimes mind and body change so rapidly that he observes them well and feels an urgent longing to face whatever is coming next. At such a time he should note the “urgency” itself; and when he feels that he is doing well, that feeling too must be noted and observed. He looks forward to progress in insight — let that “expectation” also be noted. Whatever phenomenon arises, he should observe it steadily and evenly, neither attempting any special effort nor growing slack. Often, because of urgency, rapture, clinging, or expectation, his observation retreats and loosens. Some practitioners, thinking the goal is already within reach, press forward with extraordinary exertion — yet once they do so they only grow dull again. For an unsettled mind cannot focus precisely on the phenomena of mind and body. Therefore, when observation enters smooth waters, one need only continue steadily and resolutely — neither slackening nor making special efforts — and he will soon give rise to the insight-wisdom that penetrates to the very source of mind-and-body phenomena, and realize nirvāṇa. At this stage, some meditators’ condition may rise and fall; do not let disappointment find a foothold. Rather, be firm and unwavering, noting the sensations of the six sense bases. Yet unless one can observe evenly and tranquilly, it is impossible to see all things comprehensively.

Whether the meditator begins by observing the rising and falling of the abdomen or by any other bodily or mental object, he finds that a continuous momentum is produced; then the power of observation becomes calm and fluid, flowing on unbroken without any need of deliberate attention. He watches tranquilly and clearly the ceasing of all conditioned formations, his mind free of defilement: however alluring the external world, he is unmoved by it; however irritating, it no longer brings him suffering. He sees only seeing, hears only hearing, smells only smelling, tastes only tasting, touches only touching, cognizes only cognizing. He possesses the six kinds of concentration-power recorded in the scriptures and contemplates the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, until within absorption the sense of time disappears. Once the five faculties — faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom — are balanced and complete, he will realize nirvāṇa. (Note: Here Mahāsi describes in detail the realization of nirvāṇa, but this is of little help to most practitioners; to know too much and so generate anticipation, rather than clearly observing the changing of mind and body in the present moment, is dangerous.)

After a person has realized nirvāṇa, he finds that his temperament and state of mind have changed profoundly — his whole life has been transformed. He believes unshakably in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Because his faith has strengthened, he gains joy and tranquillity, and rapture wells up within him. On first realizing nirvāṇa, owing to the intensity of that rapture, he finds he cannot observe clearly however hard he tries (note: this varies with each person’s experience). Yet after a few hours or days this experience gradually subsides, and he is able to observe clearly once more. In some meditators’ case, having tasted nirvāṇa they feel a great burden lifted and become relaxed and at ease, no longer wishing to observe; having attained their goal, their contentment within is understandable. They may go on to practice at even higher stages.

The method of insight meditation outlined in this article is more than sufficient for a person of ordinary capacity. After reading it, if one’s faith is firm, one’s longing for the Way sincere, and one’s energy untiring, and one practices step by step accordingly, progress is certain. Yet it must be said here that the details of insight experience and of the progressive stages cannot all be conveyed within so short a space; there remains much that is worth introducing and explaining. On the other hand, not every meditator’s experience follows exactly what is described here. Because of differences in capacities and karmic conditions, there are bound to be variations; and faith, resolve, and energy likewise are not all the same. Furthermore, a meditator who relies solely on reading books, with no teacher to guide him, is like a traveler setting out for the first time on an unfamiliar road — he is bound to be apprehensive, as though treading on thin ice, hesitating and uncertain. If he continues his efforts without the guidance and encouragement of a teacher, the path to realizing nirvāṇa is plainly no easy matter. In view of this difficulty, one who genuinely wishes to practice and is determined to realize nirvāṇa at all costs must seek out a teacher whose own realization and attainment are equal to the task, to lead the student through the entire course — from the most elementary stage up to the highest insight-wisdom and the realization of nirvāṇa. This advice accords well with what the scriptures say: “Seek a wise teacher from one who has truly transcended birth-and-death.”
